questions.q: Why can't a classical simulation reproduce double-slit interference just by not logging which slit each particle used?
options: Because classical simulations are too slow to compute an interference pattern

Because in such a simulation each particle still has a definite single-slit trajectory the whole time, and interference requires the physical amplitude to genuinely cover both paths at once with no definite single path existing anywhere, logged or not
Because classical simulations always produce more interference than real experiments
Because which-path information can only be erased in real experiments, never in simulations
questions.explain: The key point is that interference requires the absence of any definite single-path fact in the underlying physical description, not just the absence of a logged record. A classical simulation with definite per-particle trajectories has already removed the thing that produces interference, regardless of whether that trajectory is recorded anywhere.

questions.q: When a qubit is measured twice in a row in the same basis and gives the same result both times, which postulate explains why the second measurement is no longer probabilistic?
options: Postulate 1 (normalization)
Postulate 2 (Hermitian observables)
Postulate 4 (collapse) — the first measurement already collapsed the state to the eigenstate matching its outcome, leaving no other component to produce a different result
Postulate 5 (unitary evolution)
questions.explain: Postulate 4 states the system collapses to the eigenstate matching the observed outcome immediately after measurement. Once collapsed, a second immediate measurement in the same basis has only one component to find, so it returns the same result with certainty — this is specifically a collapse (postulate 4) effect, not normalization or evolution.

questions.q: What is the single underlying theme connecting blackbody radiation, the photoelectric effect, and atomic spectral lines, as explained in Scenario 3?
options: All three show that light always travels at the same speed
All three show that energy is not continuously divisible at the quantum scale — it shows up as frequency-sized chunks in vibrational modes, in photons, and in atomic energy levels
All three were discovered by the same scientist
All three only occur at extremely low temperatures
questions.explain: Quantization is the common thread: discrete energy exchange in vibrating modes (blackbody radiation), discrete photon energies tied to frequency (photoelectric effect), and discrete atomic energy levels (spectral lines) are three different experimental windows onto the same fact about nature.

questions.q: According to Scenario 4, why is skipping the hydrogen atom and perturbation theory not the same as skipping real quantum mechanics?
options: Because the hydrogen atom and perturbation theory are outdated and no longer considered correct physics

Because the five postulates ARE the actual content of quantum mechanics, while the hydrogen atom and perturbation theory are applications of those postulates to a specific physical system irrelevant to how quantum computers process information
Because quantum computers don't use any of the five postulates either
Because perturbation theory is actually covered later in this same course under a different name
questions.explain: The postulates are the theory; solving the hydrogen atom or applying perturbation theory are applications of that theory to specific physical systems. Skipping those specific applications, while still teaching the postulates with full rigor, is a scope decision, not an omission of the actual theory.

questions.q: In Scenario 5's synthesis, what is identified as the key structural difference between a classical bit and a qubit, tracing back through all four lessons?
options: A qubit uses more electrical power than a classical bit

A classical bit inherits classical physics's assumption of continuous, divisible quantities and definite trajectories, pinned deterministically to 0 or 1; a qubit's state is a normalized vector that can be in superposition, with measurement outcomes governed probabilistically by the Born rule and followed by collapse
A qubit can only ever store the value 0, never 1
There is no real structural difference; qubits are just slower classical bits
questions.explain: The throughline across all four lessons is that classical bits rest on classical physics's continuous, deterministic assumptions, while qubits rest on the actual quantum-mechanical postulates: normalized state vectors, superposition, probabilistic measurement via the Born rule, and collapse — the exact mechanism chapter 2 builds on.
